23875-the-relief-of-mafeking-how-it-was-:
Filson Young published The Relief of Mafeking in London in 1900, telling how Mahon's flying column accomplished it, with earlier episodes of the Boer War of 1899 to 1900. Portraits and plans accompany a narrative written within months of the events, dated July 31, 1900.

Part One covers England in time of war: how the reserves came up, how the army left England, and how the wounded came home. Later parts follow the long sea road, scenes at Cape Town, Magersfontein and Kimberley, and Paardeberg. Lord Roberts's advance to Bloemfontein and an expedition with Lord Methuen complete the march. It is a war correspondent's book, close to the action it describes.
32118-child-versus-parent-some-chapters-:
Stephen S. Wise, rabbi of the Free Synagogue, published Child Versus Parent with Macmillan in March 1922. Its subtitle names its subject: some chapters on the irrepressible conflict in the home. Wise dedicated the book to the memory of his mother, Sabine de Fischer Wise. He writes as a rabbi and public moralist, not as a laboratory psychologist, and his chapters address parents directly about the strains of family life.

The contents move from facing the problem and the roots of all conflicts, through parental responsibilities unmet and the art of parental giving, to wars that are not wars and conflicts irrepressible. Later chapters weigh conflicting standards, the democratic regime in the home, and reverence for son and daughter, before closing on the obsession of possession. Readers get an early twentieth-century plea for respect, honesty, and shared rule inside the family.

nasa-tm-19650007147-instrumentation-repo:
R W Conrad and J R Lease at Goddard Space Flight Center reported on the instruments flown on two Nike Apache sounding rockets. The flights were numbered 14.194 CA and 14.195 CA. Their report is dated February 1965, from work written in December 1964.

Conrad and Lease review the instrumentation and telemetry gear used on both flights. Sounding rockets fly brief missions, so their instruments must work at once. A report like this one records what was fitted and how it performed. Later rocket teams could use that record when planning their own flights.
nasa-tm-19660024032-convective-heat-tran:
James E Terry measured how heat flows into a blunt lifting entry body shaped like a cone with a flat face. The shape came from a family of blunt lifting bodies studied earlier by Davy and Seiff. It was designed for a best lift-to-drag ratio of about one half. Heat transfer and pressure were both mapped across its surface in the tests.

Runs covered speeds near Mach four and Mach five, with pressure also read at Mach three. Attack and sideslip angles were varied widely. At the design attitude, the measured heating pattern is reported in detail. Entry heating decides how thick a heat shield must be, so maps of this kind fed directly into vehicle design.
nasa-tm-19690004696-response-of-the-ion-:
Leo R. Davis and Andrei Konradi report the response of the ion-electron detector flown on Explorer 12, in this November 1968 Goddard paper. Explorer 12 launched on August 16, 1961, and stopped transmitting that December. Its tilted orbit carried it out through the boundary of Earth's magnetic shield twice on every circuit.

Readers get a time history of the detector's output across those months in orbit. The detector itself was a scintillation counter: a zinc sulfide crystal layer on a photomultiplier tube, under thin aluminum foil. A stepping motor wheel swung varied nickel absorber thicknesses before it, sorting incoming particles by energy. Gold discs on the wheel scattered extra flux through a second opening in some positions.
nasa-tm-19710008114-two-dimensional-casc:
Stanley M. Nosek and John F. Kline of the Lewis Research Center tested a jet-flap turbine rotor blade. The blade sat in a flat cascade of six blades for the tests. A jet flap blows air from the blade's rear edge to bend the flow.

The team studied the idea as a boundary-layer control and as a way to vary the flow area. They surveyed pressures on the blade surface at midspan. They also measured pressures and flow angles where the air left the blades. Jet flows ran from none to a small share of the main flow. The results show the force each blade made and the energy it lost.
